questions.question: Q1. What exactly is a depth map?

answers.a: A standard color photo showing surface textures
answers.b: A 2D grid where every pixel holds a distance value instead of color
answers.c: A fully finished 3D model ready for printing
answers.d: A map with GPS coordinates of where a photo was taken

explanations.a: Not quite! A regular color photo stores brightness and color. A depth map is completely different—it only cares about distance, not colors.
explanations.b: Spot on! Think of it as a regular image, but instead of RGB colors, each pixel tells you how far away that spot is. This is the raw ingredient we use to build a 3D point cloud. Learn more about depth maps
explanations.c: Nope! A depth map is just raw distance data. A 3D mesh (made of connected triangles) comes much later in the pipeline (around Experiment 7) after we've built and cleaned up our point cloud.
explanations.d: Incorrect. GPS data tells you where the camera is in the world. A depth map tells you how far objects in the scene are from the camera.

questions.question: Q2. When we turn a 2D depth map pixel into a 3D point in space, what do we call that magical process?

explanations.a: Close in name, opposite in action! Forward projection takes a 3D point and figures out where it lands on a 2D image. We used that in Experiment 2 for camera calibration, not for making point clouds.
explanations.b: You got it! Back-projection takes a 2D pixel (u, v) and its depth (Z), and uses the camera's inner quirks to reverse-engineer its actual 3D location (X, Y, Z). It literally projects the pixel 'back' into the real world. More on 3D reconstruction from depth
explanations.c: Not this time. Image segmentation is when an AI or algorithm slices an image into different objects or regions (like finding a car in a photo).
explanations.d: Nope. Color mapping is just how we paint the points (like using a heat map for depth). It's not the math that actually puts the points in 3D space.

questions.question: Q3. In our back-projection formula X = (u - cx) × Z / fx, what does the (u - cx) part actually do?

answers.a: It measures the total width of the depth image
answers.b: It finds how far the pixel is horizontally from the camera's optical center
answers.c: It represents the camera lens's focal length
answers.d: It adds some random noise to our depth measurement

explanations.a: Incorrect. The total image width is just a fixed resolution setting. Our formula calculates things pixel by pixel.
explanations.b: Exactly! It measures the horizontal offset between our pixel (u) and the camera's true center, the principal point (cx). This tells us if the point is to the left or right of the camera's center line. If the pixel is right in the middle (u = cx), then X = 0!
explanations.c: Not quite. The focal length is fx, which is the other part of the formula. (u - cx) is a pixel distance, while fx is a lens property.
explanations.d: Nope. Noise messes with our Z (depth) value before we even get to this formula. This part of the math is purely geometric.

questions.question: Q4. If your depth camera is running at 640x480 resolution and every single pixel gets a valid reading, roughly how many 3D points will pop out?

explanations.a: You just added the width and height together! We need the total area, so we multiply, not add.
explanations.b: You're off by a factor of 10! The math here is simply 640 multiplied by 480.
explanations.c: Spot on! 640 × 480 = 307,200. Since every valid pixel gives us exactly one 3D point, we get over 300,000 points. That's a lot of data from a single frame!
explanations.d: This is just the width. You can't forget about all the rows below the first one!

questions.question: Q5. According to our point spacing formula Δs = Z / fx, what happens to the distance between points as the object moves further away?

answers.a: The points get closer together, making the object look super dense
answers.b: The points spread further apart, making the object look sparse and ghost-like
answers.c: The points stay exactly the same distance apart no matter what
answers.d: The spacing becomes negative, causing points to overlap

explanations.a: Backwards! As distance (Z) goes up, the spacing (Δs) goes up too. So things get less dense, not more.
explanations.b: Correct! Because Z is in the numerator, bigger distances mean bigger gaps between your points. This is exactly why it’s so hard to capture fine details on objects that are far away from your scanner.
explanations.c: Nope! If spacing didn't care about distance, Z wouldn't even be in the formula.
explanations.d: Mathematically impossible! Z and fx are always positive numbers in the real world, so their result will always be positive too.

questions.question: Q6. What exactly does our noise model Z_measured = Z_true + N(0, σ²) tell us?

answers.a: That the camera always doubles the actual distance by mistake
answers.b: That our measured depth is the real depth plus a random error pulled from a bell curve
answers.c: That we only get noisy data if the camera or object is moving around
answers.d: That σ stands for the camera's focal length

explanations.a: Nope. This is an additive formula, meaning we are just adding a random hiccup, not multiplying the whole distance by two.
explanations.b: Exactly! It basically says 'what you measure = the real distance + a random guess from a bell curve'. It’s the standard way to admit that our sensors aren't perfect and have unbiased, random jitter. More on Gaussian noise models
explanations.c: Incorrect. This noise happens even if everything is completely frozen in place. It’s just inherent jitter in the electronics and optics.
explanations.d: Nope. σ (sigma) is the standard deviation of our noise. Focal length is fx or fy.

questions.question: Q7. In point cloud lingo, what's a 'flying pixel'?

answers.a: A scan of a bug or bird that flew past the camera
answers.b: A weird, isolated point floating between a foreground object and the background, caused by a confused sensor
answers.c: A pixel that recorded a distance of absolute zero
answers.d: The brightest, most colorful pixel in the point cloud

explanations.a: It sounds fun, but no! It has nothing to do with actual flying creatures.
explanations.b: Correct! When your camera looks at the sharp edge of an object, it gets confused between the object and the background wall. It ends up guessing a depth right in the middle, creating a rogue point that hovers in mid-air. Related depth sensing artefacts
explanations.c: Incorrect. A depth of zero usually means the sensor failed completely, and that point gets thrown out, not left floating in space.
explanations.d: Nope. Flying pixels are about distance errors, not color or brightness.

questions.question: Q8. Why is it absolutely critical to get camera calibration (Experiment 2) right before making a point cloud?

answers.a: It isn't—you can just guess a focal length and it'll be fine
answers.b: Because the back-projection math relies totally on those calibration numbers. Bad numbers mean a warped, funhouse-mirror point cloud.
answers.c: Calibration just makes the colors in the 3D viewer look nicer
answers.d: Calibration is only for stereo cameras, not regular depth sensors

explanations.a: Terrible idea! If you guess, your 3D points will be thrown all over the place.
explanations.b: Spot on. Our formulas X = (u - cx) × Z / fx depend entirely on fx, fy, cx, and cy. If these are even slightly off, every single point gets placed in the wrong spot, stretching or shrinking your 3D model. Calibration is non-negotiable!
explanations.c: Incorrect. Calibration is all about the pure geometry of the lenses, not the paint job.
explanations.d: Nope! Every single device that extracts 3D data—whether stereo, LiDAR, or structured light—needs perfect intrinsic calibration to work.

questions.question: Q9. What exactly does cloud density (ρ = N_valid / A_surface) measure?

answers.a: How heavy the point cloud file is in megabytes
answers.b: How tightly packed the points are over a physical area (like points per square meter)
answers.c: How bright or intense the colors are
answers.d: The distance from the camera to the center of the object

explanations.a: Nope! While a dense cloud means a bigger file size, this formula measures geometric density in the real world, not disk space.
explanations.b: Exactly! It’s literally just counting how many points (N_valid) are squeezed into a specific area (A_surface). High density means a rich, highly detailed scan. Low density means a sparse, dotty mess.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Density is all about spatial crowding, not visuals.
explanations.d: Nope. Distance is Z. Density is about how many points cover a specific patch of surface at that distance.

questions.question: Q10. Which of these 3D scanning setups produce point clouds as their main output?

answers.a: Only expensive laser LiDARs; everything else skips straight to meshes
answers.b: Pretty much all of them! LiDAR, structured light, and stereo cameras all generate point clouds.
answers.c: Point clouds are just for video games, real engineers don't use them
answers.d: They are just a visualization trick on the screen, not real data

explanations.a: Nope. LiDAR definitely uses them, but so does almost every other 3D tech.
explanations.b: Correct! Point clouds are the universal language of 3D scanning. Whether you're shooting lasers (LiDAR), projecting patterns (structured light), or using two cameras (stereo), the raw output is always a point cloud. Making a mesh comes later!
explanations.c: Couldn't be further from the truth. Engineers, doctors, archaeologists, and self-driving cars all rely heavily on point clouds.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Point clouds are raw, hard mathematical data representing physical reality. They are definitely not just a display trick.
